summary: Detailed documentation of UCSB's Remote Job Service, following up on RFC 436. It restates the essence of the official RJE protocol in RFC 407 and describes the subset UCSB implemented, listing what was not supported. A rewrite was planned for about six months later.

eli5.summary: A manual for a university computer that took jobs sent over the network, including a list of the things it could not yet do.

subtitle: Complete documentation of UCSB's implementation of remote job submission over the network.

tldr.problem: Universities with batch processing systems needed to let remote users submit and monitor jobs over the ARPANET. Each site had to implement the RJE protocol differently.
tldr.mechanism: UCSB's Remote Job Service provides a HASP virtual RJE terminal to each authenticated user, maintaining the association between the user and their batch jobs. It supports both a formal standard command syntax and a user-friendly local syntax.
tldr.outcome: RFC 477 documents UCSB's subset implementation of the RJE protocol and its extensions. A rewrite was planned to address known limitations like abandoning jobs on errors.

today: RFC 477 documents a working batch job submission service from 1973. HASP is obsolete; modern batch systems use different protocols. UCSB's RJS is no longer in service.

sections.title: Remote Job Service Overview
sections.content:
UCSB's Remote Job Service (RJS), documented in RFC 477, provides network-based access to the IBM 360/75 batch processing system running OS MVT release 21.0 and HASP. RJS acts as an interface between remote users and the HASP job queuing system, offering each user a virtual remote job entry terminal consisting of a card reader, card punch, line printer, and operator's console.

The service implements a subset of the official RJE protocol specified in RFC 407. Known limitations include no RJE control card checking, no job batching in input files, limited output dispositions, and no restart markers. However, the document emphasizes UCSB's openness to suggestions for improvements.
sections.eli5: A system that let scientists at another university send batch jobs to UCSB's big computer over the network, watch them run, and get the results back.

sections.title: Authentication and Job Management
sections.content:
A user begins by logging in with a user name, password, and account number. This accounting information identifies the owner of a particular HASP virtual RJE terminal. Each user name remains associated with one terminal. A user may own multiple jobs (currently up to 5) simultaneously, and can track their status even after logging out and back in, possibly from a different site.

Jobs can complete normally after storage of the last output, or abnormally at any stage. The circumstances of final disposition are displayed to the user if logged in, saved for a period afterward, and available on request at next login. Status information is retained for at least a fixed period (currently two days).
sections.eli5: Each scientist gets an account and can send multiple jobs to the queue at once. They can check on the jobs later, even from a different computer.

sections.title: Two Command Syntaxes
sections.content:
RJS supports two command syntaxes. The standard syntax strictly follows the official RJE protocol with commands like USER, PASS, ACCT, INPATH, OUTPATH, INPUT, CANCEL, and STATUS. This syntax is cumbersome for human users but ideal for programs.

The local syntax provides a more natural interface inspired by common systems like UNIX. It supports commands like LOGIN, SOURCE, PRINT, PUNCH, DELETE, JOBSTAT, and JOBLIST. The local syntax also adds convenience features: INUSER and INACCT as aliases, and the ability to issue HASP operator commands directly through a virtual console using the dollar sign prefix (e.g., $ SDJ jobid).
sections.eli5: RJS understood two different ways to write commands: one strict way for computer programs, and one casual way that seemed more natural to people typing at a terminal.

sections.title: File Transfer Modes
sections.content:
The pathname parameter specifies file locations and attributes for source, print, and punch files. A pathname can reference either a socket (for simplex connection) or a file via FTP. Data attributes control carriage control (TELNET, ASA, or none) and data code (ASCII or EBCDIC).

For simplex connections, the server opens the connection itself. For FTP, RJS acts as an FTP client, issuing USER, PASS, ACCT, BYTE, ALLO, RETR and STOR commands to the remote FTP server. The combination of carriage control mode and data code determines how records are formatted and transferred.
sections.eli5: Jobs can get data from distant files, and results can be sent back to distant computers. Different data formats and transfer methods are supported.
